claim: Pyramidal neurons receive inputs from various areas onto their morphologically distinct apical and basal trees.
source: Pyramidal neurons, a mainstay of cortical regions, receive a plethora of inputs from various areas onto their morphologically distinct apical and basal trees.
evidence: This is a general statement about pyramidal neuron anatomy and connectivity, drawing from established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Apical and basal trees differentially contribute to the somatic response, defining distinct anatomical and possibly functional sub-units.
source: Both trees differentially contribute to the somatic response, defining distinct anatomical and possibly functional sub-units.
evidence: This is a general statement about dendritic tree function, drawing from established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: The model replicates electrophysiological and two-photon imaging data.
source: Towards this goal, we used a morphologically detailed computational model of a single cell that replicates electrophysiological and two-photon imaging data.
evidence: The manuscript describes validation of the model against experimental data.

claim: Basal tree activity is necessary for producing somatic activity.
source: Our simulations predict a synergistic effect of apical and basal trees on somatic action potential generation: basal tree activity, in the form of either depolarization or dendritic spiking, is necessary for producing somatic activity, despite the fact that most somatic spikes are heavily driven by apical dendritic spikes.
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational model simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Most somatic spikes are heavily driven by apical dendritic spikes.
source: Our simulations predict a synergistic effect of apical and basal trees on somatic action potential generation: basal tree activity, in the form of either depolarization or dendritic spiking, is necessary for producing somatic activity, despite the fact that most somatic spikes are heavily driven by apical dendritic spikes.
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational model simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Layer 2 and 3 pyramidal neurons conform to a stereotypical morphology characterized by separate apical and basal dendritic arbors.
source: In the primary visual cortex (V1), layer 2 and 3 (L2/3) pyramidal neurons conform to a stereotypical morphology characterized by separate apical and basal dendritic arbors.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about L2/3 pyramidal neuron morphology in neuroscience.

claim: The apical tree consists of a thick apical trunk that extends into L1 and splits into an apical tuft.
source: The apical tree consists of a thick apical trunk that extends into L1 and splits into an apical tuft.
evidence: This is a description of apical tree morphology based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: The basal tree consists of numerous dendritic segments, the majority of which sprout directly from the base of the soma.
source: The basal tree consists of numerous dendritic segments, the majority of which sprout directly from the base of the soma, indicating that they can directly influence somatic output (Spruston, 2008).
evidence: This is a description of basal tree morphology supported by a citation.

claim: Basal dendrites can directly influence somatic output.
source: The basal tree consists of numerous dendritic segments, the majority of which sprout directly from the base of the soma, indicating that they can directly influence somatic output (Spruston, 2008).
evidence: This is an inference from morphology supported by a citation.

claim: Layer 4 and L2/3 pyramidal neurons synapse with basal dendrites of L2/3 pyramidal neurons, providing them with feedforward input.
source: layer 4 (L4) and L2/3 pyramidal neurons synapse with basal dendrites of L2/3 pyramidal neurons, providing them with feedforward input (Coogan and Burkhalter, 1990; Larkum, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about neural connectivity supported by citations.

claim: The apical dendrites of L2/3 pyramidal neurons receive feedback input from higher order areas of the cortex such as the secondary and tertiary visual cortices, lateromedial area and prefrontal cortex.
source: The apical dendrites of the L2/3 pyramidal neurons instead receive feedback input from higher order areas of the cortex such as the secondary and tertiary visual cortices, lateromedial area and prefrontal cortex (Coogan and Burkhalter, 1990; Larkum, 2013), as well as orientation-tuned thalamocortical input (Chen et al., 2013; Cruz-Martín et al., 2014; Jia et al., 2010; Roth et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about neural connectivity supported by citations.

claim: The apical dendrites of L2/3 pyramidal neurons receive orientation-tuned thalamocortical input.
source: The apical dendrites of the L2/3 pyramidal neurons instead receive feedback input from higher order areas of the cortex such as the secondary and tertiary visual cortices, lateromedial area and prefrontal cortex (Coogan and Burkhalter, 1990; Larkum, 2013), as well as orientation-tuned thalamocortical input (Chen et al., 2013; Cruz-Martín et al., 2014; Jia et al., 2010; Roth et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about neural connectivity supported by citations.

claim: Apical and basal trees have distinct biophysical properties.
source: These anatomical and connectivity features of the apical and basal trees, complemented by their distinct biophysical properties (Cho et al., 2008), shape both the local dendritic processing and the integration of the two input streams at the soma.
evidence: This is a statement about biophysical properties supported by a citation.

claim: Single spines of L2/3 pyramidal neurons exhibit orientation selectivity.
source: These studies have shown that single spines of L2/3 pyramidal neurons exhibit orientation selectivity, with synaptic orientation preferences varying even on the same branch (Iacaruso et al., 2017; Jia et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about spine properties supported by citations.

claim: Synaptic orientation preferences vary even on the same branch.
source: These studies have shown that single spines of L2/3 pyramidal neurons exhibit orientation selectivity, with synaptic orientation preferences varying even on the same branch (Iacaruso et al., 2017; Jia et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about synaptic properties supported by citations.

claim: Blockage of dendritic sodium and NMDA activity leads to impaired or abolished orientation selectivity at the level of the soma.
source: Older modeling work has established that blockage of dendritic sodium and NMDA activity leads to impaired or abolished orientation selectivity at the level of the soma (Archie and Mel, 2000; Mel et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a statement about modeling results supported by citations.

claim: Individual dendritic segments of L2/3 neurons generate nonlinear regenerative responses, termed dendritic spikes, independently of the soma.
source: It is also known that individual dendritic segments of L2/3 neurons generate nonlinear regenerative responses, termed dendritic spikes, independently of the soma, making their exact contribution to somatic output unclear (Palmer et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about dendritic properties supported by citations.

claim: Strong, sparse inputs to the dendrites are sufficient to drive somatic output.
source: On the other hand, it was recently proposed that strong, sparse inputs to the dendrites are sufficient to drive somatic output (Goetz et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about dendritic input-output relationships supported by a citation.

claim: Dendritic spikes in the apical tuft of L2/3 V1 pyramidal neurons influence orientation selectivity.
source: Interestingly, although dendritic spikes in the apical tuft of L2/3 V1 pyramidal neurons influence orientation selectivity (Goetz et al., 2021; Smith et al., 2013), this orientation selectivity is robust to ablation of the apical tree (Park et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about dendritic spike function supported by citations.

claim: Orientation selectivity is robust to ablation of the apical tree.
source: Interestingly, although dendritic spikes in the apical tuft of L2/3 V1 pyramidal neurons influence orientation selectivity (Goetz et al., 2021; Smith et al., 2013), this orientation selectivity is robust to ablation of the apical tree (Park et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about experimental results supported by a citation.

claim: The model is based on the L2/3 V1 pyramidal cell model of Park et al., 2019.
source: The single neuron model is based on the L2/3 V1 pyramidal cell model of Park et al., 2019 created in the NEURON simulation environment (Hines and Carnevale, 2001).
evidence: This is a statement about the model's origin supported by citations.

claim: The model was created in the NEURON simulation environment.
source: The single neuron model is based on the L2/3 V1 pyramidal cell model of Park et al., 2019 created in the NEURON simulation environment (Hines and Carnevale, 2001).
evidence: This is a statement about the modeling platform supported by a citation.

claim: The model's electrophysiological properties were validated against experimental data.
source: As the model makes use of a variety of passive and active mechanisms ( Tables 1–4), its electrophysiological properties were validated against experimental data (Park et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about model validation supported by a citation.

claim: Apical stimulus-driven synaptic inputs have had a 10ms delay added to better reflect experimental data on feedback synaptic inputs.
source: Apical stimulus-driven synaptic inputs have had a 10ms delay added, to better reflect experimental data on feedback synaptic inputs (Ju et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about model parameters supported by a citation.

claim: Simulations with synchronous activation of the apical and basal synaptic inputs resulted in qualitatively similar results.
source: Simulations with synchronous activation of the apical and basal synaptic inputs resulted in qualitatively similar results (data not shown).
evidence: This is a statement about simulation results from the model.

claim: All simulations were performed on a High-Performance Computing Cluster with 624 cores and 3.328 TB of shared RAM under CentOS 7.4 OS.
source: All simulations were performed on our High-Performance Computing Cluster (Rocks 7.0) with 624 cores and 3.328 TB of shared RAM under CentOS 7.4 OS (Papadopoulos et al., 2003), through the NEURON simulation environment (Hines and Carnevale, 2001).
evidence: This is a statement about the computational infrastructure used.

claim: Model neuron output measurements were obtained at a sampling rate of 10 KHz (dt = 0.1ms).
source: Model neuron output measurements were obtained at a sampling rate of 10 KHz (dt = 0.1ms).
evidence: This is a statement about the simulation parameters.

claim: Simulation duration was 2500 ms, with stimulus onset at t = 500 ms.
source: Simulation duration was 2500 ms, with stimulus onset (where present) at t = 500 ms.
evidence: This is a statement about the simulation parameters.

claim: All experimental protocols were approved by Brigham and Women's Hospital Institution Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: All experimental protocols were approved by Brigham and Women's Hospital (BWH) Institution Animal Care and Use Committee.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for experiments.

claim: Male and female wild-type (C57BL/6) mice were purchased from The Jackson Laboratory and bred for experiments.
source: Male and female wild-type (C57BL/6) mice were purchased from The Jackson Laboratory and bred for experiments.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental subjects.

claim: A total of 2 mice were used in these experiments, with recordings from 11 neurons used for data analysis.
source: A total of 2 mice were used in these experiments, with recordings from 11 neurons used for data analysis.
evidence: This is a statement about the sample size.

claim: The model can produce realistic dendritic spikes.
source: Results show that the model can produce realistic dendritic spikes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D), while the properties of the spiking events vary between dendritic segments (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is a statement about model output supported by figures.

claim: The properties of the spiking events vary between dendritic segments.
source: Results show that the model can produce realistic dendritic spikes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D), while the properties of the spiking events vary between dendritic segments (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is a statement about model output supported by figures.

claim: Both apical and basal dendritic segments exhibit a large degree of variation in their spiking thresholds.
source: Both apical and basal dendritic segments exhibit a large degree of variation in their spiking thresholds (Figure 1E, F; threshold synapse count mean and standard deviations: basal 12.286±6.649 sodium, 51.429 ± 13.179 NMDA; apical 14.442 ± 13.825 sodium, 40.721 ± 23.675 NMDA).
evidence: This is a statement about model output supported by figures and quantitative data.

claim: Dendritic segments with high sodium spiking thresholds also tended to exhibit higher NMDA spiking thresholds.
source: Dendritic segments with high sodium spiking thresholds also tended to exhibit higher NMDA spiking thresholds.
evidence: This is an observation from the model data.

claim: All dendritic segments of the model neuron exhibit non-linear input-output functions.
source: Results indicate that all dendritic segments of the model neuron exhibit non-linear input-output functions (Figure 1D, NRLE = 1 denotes linear, NRLE <1 sublinear, and NRLE >1 supralinear), in line with experimental observations (Smith et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about model output supported by figures and citations.

claim: The NRLE values are relatively widely dispersed, providing a large dynamic range of possible dendrite-level computations.
source: In addition, the NRLE values are relatively widely dispersed (values ranging from >1 to~3.5), providing a large dynamic range of possible dendrite-level computations.
evidence: This is an observation from the model data with an inference about computational implications.

claim: There is diversity in apical and basal dendritic integration that can be exploited to modulate orientation tuning.
source: The above results show that there is diversity in apical and basal dendritic integration that can be exploited to modulate orientation tuning.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: The sodium spiking propensity varies as a function of dendritic segment volume and electrotonic length.
source: The above differences are, at least in part, due to the morphological and electrophysiological features of dendritic segments, as we found that the sodium spiking propensity varies as a function of dendritic segment volume and electrotonic length (see Figure 5).
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by a figure.

claim: Spontaneous activity patterns in the model are very similar to those seen in two-photon calcium imaging data.
source: We found that spontaneous activity patterns in the model are very similar to those seen in two-photon calcium imaging data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is a statement about model validation supported by figures.

claim: The model neuron is well-tuned (OSI >0.2, tuning width <80°).
source: The resulting orientation tuning curve (preferred orientation firing rate: 1.55 ± 0.3 Hz, orthogonal orientation firing rate: 0.21 ± 0.12 Hz, OSI 0.77 ± 0.11, tuning width 44 ± 9.17°; Figure 2A) indicates that the model neuron is well-tuned (OSI >0.2, tuning width <80°; see Extended methods, Orientation tuning validation protocol), in agreement with our prior work using the original version of this model (Park et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about model output supported by quantitative data and a figure.

claim: Orientation tuning persists post-ablation of the apical tree.
source: We also reproduced the apical tree ablation experiment from that publication, finding that orientation tuning does indeed persist post-ablation (Figure 2—figure supplement 5; see Extended methods, Ablation protocol).
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by a figure.

claim: The model neuron diverges from the expected orientation preference and exhibits a bias towards the preferred orientation of the basal tree.
source: We found that the model neuron diverges from the expected orientation preference (linear summation of synaptic inputs) and exhibits a bias towards the preferred orientation of the basal tree.
evidence: This is a statement about model results.

claim: The model neuron did not exhibit adequate tuning beyond a dendritic disparity of 50°.
source: Of note, the model neuron did not exhibit adequate tuning (i.e. 20% or more of neurons featured OSI <0.2 or tuning width >80°; see Extended methods, Orientation tuning validation protocol) beyond a dendritic disparity of 50°.
evidence: This is a statement about model results.

claim: The deviation from expectation displayed by the neuron appears to be decreased in the 'even' model.
source: We found that, indeed, the deviation from expectation displayed by the neuron appears to be decreased in the 'even' model, and is clearly reversed in the 'inverse biologically plausible' model.
evidence: This is a statement about model results.

claim: The deviation from expectation is clearly reversed in the 'inverse biologically plausible' model.
source: We found that, indeed, the deviation from expectation displayed by the neuron appears to be decreased in the 'even' model, and is clearly reversed in the 'inverse biologically plausible' model.
evidence: This is a statement about model results.

claim: Apical and basal synaptic inputs are not linearly combined, but rather interact in a non-linear manner to produce somatic output.
source: Overall, the observed deviation from expectation indicates that apical and basal synaptic inputs are not linearly combined, but rather interact in a non-linear manner to produce somatic output.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: The interaction between apical and basal inputs is influenced by the synaptic distribution along the two dendritic trees, as well as their mean synaptic orientation preferences.
source: This interaction is influenced by the synaptic distribution along the two dendritic trees, as well as their mean synaptic orientation preferences.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: The majority of somatic spikes are dependent on apical sodium conductance.
source: We find that the majority of somatic spikes are dependent on apical sodium conductance (N=131 spikes; apically driven 76.51 ± 10.21%, basally driven 9.61 ± 5.03%, cooperative 13.89 ± 11.22%; Figure 3B), which is surprising, considering the proximity of the basal dendrites to the soma, as well as the salient nature of the feedforward, visually evoked inputs received by the basal tree.
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by quantitative data and a figure.

claim: The dependence of somatic spiking activity on dendritic sodium conductance does not significantly differ between instances of stimulus-driven and background-driven activity.
source: We found that the resulting percentages are similar to the previous condition (N=25 spikes; apically driven 71.07 ± 31.56%, basally driven 17.5 ± 22.5%, cooperative 1.43 ± 4.29%; Figure 3D), indicating that the dependence of somatic spiking activity on dendritic sodium conductance does not significantly differ between instances of stimulus-driven and background-driven activity.
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by quantitative data and a figure.

claim: The distribution of background-driven synapses does not significantly affect somatic spike generation.
source: Presenting a stimulus of the preferred orientation (0°) under these conditions (case #3), we find that the resulting percentages (N=156 spikes; apically driven 85.08 ± 7.34%, basally driven 5.15 ± 6.72%, cooperative 9.78 ± 8.17%; Figure 3C) are similar to those seen in case #1, indicating that the distribution of background-driven synapses does not significantly affect somatic spike generation.
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by quantitative data and a figure.

claim: Somatic spike generation reliably depends on apical sodium conductance.
source: These simulations predict that somatic spike generation reliably depends on apical sodium conductance, a seemingly counterintuitive finding, as feedforward stimulus-driven input reaches mostly the basal tree and not the apical tree.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model results.

claim: The neuron remains tuned when stimulus-driven input is removed from either the apical or the basal tree, albeit with significantly decreased OSI values.
source: We find that the neuron remains tuned in all cases, albeit with significantly decreased OSI values (dependent two-sample t-test, control vs basal: p ≈ 0.000037; control vs apical: p ≈ 0.000007) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by statistical tests and a figure.

claim: Removal of apical stimulus-driven input has a much smaller effect on tuning than removal of basal input.
source: Removal of apical stimulus-driven input has a much smaller effect on tuning than removal of basal input (dependent two-sample t-test, apical vs basal: p ≈ 0.0095), which is in line with our previous findings (Park et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by statistical tests and a citation.

claim: Somatic tuning is completely abolished when manipulating the basal but not the apical synaptic weights.
source: We find that somatic tuning is completely abolished when manipulating the basal but not the apical synaptic weights, although tuning is significantly affected by loss of apical inputs as well (Figure 4B; dependent two-sample t-test, control vs apical: p ≈ 0.00065).
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by statistical tests and a figure.

claim: Synaptic input from the basal tree is critical for orientation tuning.
source: These results indicate that synaptic input from the basal tree is critical for orientation tuning, while apical tree synaptic inputs play a less important role.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: Sodium conductance nullification in the apical tree completely abolishes orientation tuning.
source: In line with our previous results (Figure 3), we find that sodium conductance nullification in the apical tree completely abolishes orientation tuning (Figure 4C) while the same manipulation in the basal tree has no impact on tuning (dependent two-sample t-test, control vs basal: p ≈ 0.24125).
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by statistical tests and a figure.

claim: Sodium conductance nullification in the basal tree has no impact on tuning.
source: In line with our previous results (Figure 3), we find that sodium conductance nullification in the apical tree completely abolishes orientation tuning (Figure 4C) while the same manipulation in the basal tree has no impact on tuning (dependent two-sample t-test, control vs basal: p ≈ 0.24125).
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by statistical tests and a figure.

claim: A 5% decrease in apical sodium conductance results in elimination of the apical but not the basal sodium component resulting in total loss of tuning.
source: For a decrease of 5%, we found that elimination of the apical but not the basal sodium component results in total loss of tuning (dependent two-sample t-test, control vs basal p-value: 0.32549).
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by statistical tests.

claim: In the 5% reduction scenario, the apical tree remains the primary driver of somatic activity as the majority of somatic spikes are apically driven.
source: Importantly, in this scenario the apical tree remains the primary driver of somatic activity as the majority of somatic spikes are apically driven (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A N=345 spikes; 60 ± 15% of spikes are apically driven, 30 ± 18% are basally driven, and 10 ± 8% of spikes are cooperatively driven, for details on the characterization of spiking activity, see Results, Apical sodium spikes are the primary driver of neuronal output).
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by quantitative data and a figure.

claim: A 10% decrease in the apical sodium conductance results in total loss of tuning when either the apical or the basal sodium component is eliminated.
source: However, a 10% decrease in the apical sodium conductance results in total loss of tuning when either the apical or the basal sodium component is eliminated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by a figure.

claim: The reduction in apical sodium conductance results in a decrease of the overall spiking rate of the neuron.
source: The above simulations show that, as expected, the reduction in apical sodium conductance results in a decrease of the overall spiking rate of the neuron (number of spikes: 885 in the unchanged condition, 345 for the 5% reduction, and 190 for the 10% reduction).
evidence: This is a statement about model results.

claim: Apical sodium channels are necessary for both spike generation in general as well as for orientation tuning in particular.
source: Overall, our simulations predict that apical sodium channels are necessary for both spike generation in general (Figure 3) as well as for orientation tuning in particular (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model results supported by figures.

claim: AMPA and NMDA activity is necessary for both apical and basal trees.
source: Additionally, AMPA and NMDA activity is necessary for both apical and basal trees (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by figures.

claim: The apical tree most likely exerts its influence on somatic spiking via sodium-mediated spiking.
source: This means that the apical tree most likely exerts its influence on somatic spiking via sodium-mediated spiking, whereas the basal tree mostly utilizes AMPA- and NMDA-driven depolarizations, rather than sodium spikes.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: The basal tree mostly utilizes AMPA- and NMDA-driven depolarizations, rather than sodium spikes.
source: This means that the apical tree most likely exerts its influence on somatic spiking via sodium-mediated spiking, whereas the basal tree mostly utilizes AMPA- and NMDA-driven depolarizations, rather than sodium spikes.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: EPSP attenuation is greater in apical versus basal dendritic segments of similar length.
source: We found that EPSP attenuation is greater in apical versus basal dendritic segments of similar length (Figure 5A; p-value 0.000002), diameter (Figure 5B; p-value 0.005864), or volume (data not shown; p-value 0.000001).
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by statistical tests and figures.

claim: EPSP attenuation is greater in apical versus basal dendritic segments of similar diameter.
source: We found that EPSP attenuation is greater in apical versus basal dendritic segments of similar length (Figure 5A; p-value 0.000002), diameter (Figure 5B; p-value 0.005864), or volume (data not shown; p-value 0.000001).
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by statistical tests and figures.

claim: EPSP attenuation is greater in apical versus basal dendritic segments of similar volume.
source: We found that EPSP attenuation is greater in apical versus basal dendritic segments of similar length (Figure 5A; p-value 0.000002), diameter (Figure 5B; p-value 0.005864), or volume (data not shown; p-value 0.000001).
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by statistical tests.

claim: When normalized by distance from the soma, dendritic path volume, or electrotonic length, EPSP attenuation did not significantly differ between apical and basal dendritic segments.
source: When normalized by distance from the soma (data not shown; p-value 0.42941), dendritic path volume (data not shown; p-value 0.027934), or electrotonic length (data not shown; p-value 0.666959), EPSP attenuation did not significantly differ between apical and basal dendritic segments.
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by statistical tests.

claim: Dendritic sodium spiking thresholds are significantly lower for apical versus basal dendritic segments with approximately equivalent values of electrotonic length.
source: We found that dendritic sodium spiking thresholds are significantly lower for apical versus basal dendritic segments with approximately equivalent values of electrotonic length (Figure 5C; p-value 0.001585), but this relationship is reversed for dendritic segments with similar volume (Figure 5D; p-value 0.000002).
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by statistical tests and figures.

claim: The relationship between sodium spiking thresholds and morphology is reversed for dendritic segments with similar volume.
source: We found that dendritic sodium spiking thresholds are significantly lower for apical versus basal dendritic segments with approximately equivalent values of electrotonic length (Figure 5C; p-value 0.001585), but this relationship is reversed for dendritic segments with similar volume (Figure 5D; p-value 0.000002).
evidence: This is a statement about model results supported by statistical tests and figures.

claim: The attenuation of signals originating in morphologically and electrophysiologically equivalent dendritic segments is significantly larger for apical vs. basal dendrites.
source: Taken together, this analysis shows that – as expected – the attenuation of signals originating in morphologically and electrophysiologically equivalent dendritic segments is significantly larger for apical vs. basal dendrites, likely because most apical dendrites are located further away from the soma.
evidence: This is a summary statement about model results with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: The threshold for inducing sodium spikes in apical dendritic segments is significantly smaller compared to basal dendritic segments of similar electrotonic length.
source: However, the threshold for inducing sodium spikes in apical dendritic segments is significantly smaller compared to basal dendritic segments of similar electrotonic length (most likely due to the proximity of the soma, causing a 'current sink' effect for basal dendrites), making it easier to drive such spikes in the apical compared to the basal tree.
evidence: This is a statement about model results with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: The model exhibits a wide range of non-linear behavior at the dendritic segment level.
source: In this work, we used a detailed biophysical model of a L2/3 V1 pyramidal cell (Park et al., 2019), to tease apart the relative contributions of apical vs. basal dendritic trees in somatic orientation tuning. We start by examining the threshold and strength of dendritic non-linearities, which are found to vary along the apical and basal dendrites.
evidence: This is a summary statement about model results.

claim: Dendritic and somatic spontaneous activity patterns in the model adequately reproduce experimental data.
source: By comparing model output to in vivo two-photon calcium fluorescence imaging data, we find that dendritic and somatic spontaneous activity patterns in the model adequately reproduce experimental data.
evidence: This is a statement about model validation.

claim: The tuned output of the model does not always match the linear summation of tuned input.
source: We find that the tuned output of the model does not always match the linear summation of tuned input, instead deviating towards orientation preferences more closely matching either the apical or basal mean orientation preference.
evidence: This is a statement about model results.

claim: The majority of stimulus-driven somatic spiking activity is dependent on sodium spikes generated in the apical tree.
source: We find that the majority of stimulus-driven somatic spiking activity is dependent on sodium spikes generated in the apical tree, suggesting that apical and basal trees contribute via different mechanisms to tuned somatic output.
evidence: This is a statement about model results with an inference.

claim: Apical sodium channels are critical for proper neuronal tuning.
source: Results indicate that apical sodium channels are critical for proper neuronal tuning, while basal sodium channels do not play as significant a role.
evidence: This is a statement about model results.

claim: Basal sodium channels do not play as significant a role in neuronal tuning.
source: Results indicate that apical sodium channels are critical for proper neuronal tuning, while basal sodium channels do not play as significant a role.
evidence: This is a statement about model results.

claim: AMPA and NMDA activity of both the apical and basal trees is required for orientation tuning at the level of the soma.
source: Conversely, AMPA and NMDA activity of both the apical and basal trees is required for orientation tuning at the level of the soma.
evidence: This is a statement about model results.

claim: Basal dendritic branches feature higher sodium spiking thresholds for similar electrotonic length values compared to apical branches.
source: A potential reason for this is that basal dendritic branches feature higher sodium spiking thresholds for similar electrotonic constant-normalized length values (i.e. 'electrotonic length') compared to apical branches, reducing their propensity to generate sodium spikes compared to apical dendrites.
evidence: This is a statement about model results with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Somatic spikes are only reliably produced when apical dendritic sodium spikes coincide with basal synaptically driven depolarizations and/or spikes.
source: Overall, our simulations suggest a synergistic effect between apical and basal trees, as somatic spikes are only reliably produced when apical dendritic sodium spikes coincide with basal synaptically driven depolarizations and/or spikes.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model results.

claim: Apical and basal dendrites contribute to neuronal function using different mechanisms, ionic or synaptic, which together drive action potential generation.
source: In this manner, apical and basal dendrites contribute to neuronal function using different mechanisms, ionic or synaptic, which together drive action potential generation in this neuronal type.
evidence: This is a summary statement about model results.

claim: The model predicts that somatic output in L2/3 V1 pyramidal neurons is likely to be determined through Bimodal Input Coincidence.
source: Taken together, our model predicts that somatic output in L2/3 V1 pyramidal neurons is likely to be determined through Bimodal Input Coincidence, a subcategory of coincidence detection (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model results supported by a figure.

claim: The basal tree receives visual feedforward input, representing the information as a series of hyperpolarizations, depolarizations, and occasional dendritic spikes.
source: Specifically, we propose that the basal tree receives visual feedforward input, representing the information therein as a series of hyperpolarizations, depolarizations, and occasional dendritic spikes.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on model results.

claim: Predictive and attentional signals from higher-order cortical areas reach the apical tree of the neuron, causing the generation of dendritic spikes.
source: At the same time, predictive and attentional signals from higher-order cortical areas reach the apical tree of the neuron, causing the generation of dendritic spikes that propagate to the soma and are temporally summed with any concurrent basal depolarization.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on model results and known connectivity.

claim: Apical dendrite ablation is assumed to be accompanied by homeostatic alterations that counteract the increase in input resistance from the loss of the apical tree.
source: What is seen as a contradiction is resolved by considering that in both Park et al., 2019 and the simulations presented here, apical dendrite ablation is assumed to be accompanied by homeostatic alterations that counteract the increase in input resistance from the loss of the apical tree.
evidence: This is a statement about model assumptions supported by a citation.

claim: L2/3 V1 pyramidal cells may perform salient feature extraction from visual input compatible with predictive coding.
source: Our findings suggest that L2/3 V1 pyramidal cells may perform salient feature extraction from visual input compatible with predictive coding (Rao and Ballard, 1999).
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of model results supported by a citation.

claim: Top-down signals reflecting attentional or predictive processes reach the apical tree and 'highlight' appropriate parts of the signal 'landscape' generated by the visual input reaching the basal trees.
source: When top-down signals reflecting attentional or predictive processes reach the apical tree, they 'highlight' appropriate parts of the signal 'landscape' generated by the visual input reaching the basal trees through the generation of apical dendritic sodium spikes.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on model results.
